verses.note: Abram's scruple does not become a burden he lays on others. As the leader of the expedition he treats his treaty partners fairly, giving them their due share, a principle David later makes law for those who stay behind with the baggage (1 Samuel 30:24-25).

Whatever Jacob's motives, his stated principle is sound: a leader sets the pace by the weakest member of the company, not the strongest. Scripture later pictures God himself leading his flock this way (Isaiah 40:11).

Judah begins to lead by telling his father an unwelcome truth. He does not flatter Jacob's grief or hide the terms; he names the cost of refusal. This is the first step in the change that will make Judah the family's spokesman in chapter 44.
Judah leads by stepping into the place of danger himself, not by commanding others. The brother who once proposed the sale of Joseph now stands between the ruler and the youngest brother.

Moses has the right sympathies but no recognized authority, and the question ‘who made you?’ is exactly the right question. The answer will come at the burning bush: God makes him ruler. Stephen presents this rejection as the first of many in which Israel refused the deliverer God sent (Acts 7:35).

Israel's great leaders are repeatedly taken from shepherding, Moses here and David later (Psalm 78:70-72). The Psalms remember that God led his people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron (Psalm 77:20), so the years with Jethro's sheep are part of his preparation.
Moses' authority does not rest on his eloquence or on the people's response. God's answer to discouragement is to repeat the commission, which is where a leader's confidence has to be grounded.
David's rule is described as God's appointment of a shepherd over God's people. Kingship in Israel is a stewardship; the people remain ‘my people’ throughout the oracle.

The stanza places special blame on those who guide. Leaders and prophets who tell comfortable lies do not only fall themselves; they swallow up those who follow. Scripture holds teachers to a stricter judgment (James 3:1) for this reason.
Israel's kings were meant to be shepherds and often failed (Ezekiel 34:1-10). God himself takes up the task, and Jesus claims it as the good shepherd who knows his sheep (John 10:11-14).
The confession names rulers first among the guilty. Leaders do not stand outside the nation's sin to condemn it; Scripture holds them more accountable, not less.

Jesus gives new names that point to new roles, as God renamed Abram and Jacob. The list includes a tax collector who served Rome's client ruler and a man called the zealous one, so the Twelve held together people whose politics would have kept them apart anywhere else.

Jesus defines leadership among his people against the pattern of political power. Authority in the church is real, but it is exercised as service, and the one who wants to be first must make himself the slave of all. 1 Peter 5:3 repeats the same verb in warning elders against lording it over the flock.

Those who teach others reproduce themselves in their followers. In Matthew 15:14 the blind guides are the Pharisees; in Luke the saying falls on the disciples, who will become teachers and must first be taught.

Greatness among Jesus' followers is measured by the welcome given to those with no status, and the one who counts himself least is great. Luke repeats the lesson at the Last Supper, when the same dispute arises and Jesus says he is among them as one who serves (22:24-27).

Those who teach others are judged by whether they share the weight they impose. The woe addresses every teacher of God's word, including the church's, and asks whether their teaching lifts burdens or adds them.

A teacher's failure is double: failing to enter and keeping others out. Jesus holds religious leaders responsible not only for their own response to God but for the access they give or deny to others.

Those entrusted with others are servants set over servants, charged to feed them faithfully while the master is away. The parable defines church leadership as stewardship on behalf of an absent Lord, not ownership.
The failed manager abuses those in his care and indulges himself. The warning is aimed at anyone with authority in the household of God, whose treatment of others is judged by the returning Lord.
The closing proverb falls hardest on those given much, including those entrusted with teaching and leading. James applies the same principle to teachers, who will be judged more strictly (James 3:1).

The leaders recognize the truth about themselves and respond by trying to silence its speaker. The parable is addressed to all who hold God's people in trust, and the leaders' reaction shows the danger of that trust: the stewards come to treat the vineyard as their own.

Jesus warns against leaders whose religion becomes a means to honor. Luke has already shown Jesus teaching the lowest place at banquets (14:7-11) and telling his disciples that the greatest must be like the youngest (22:26), which he will say at the Last Supper within days.

Jesus does not abolish leadership; he assumes there will be ‘the one who leads’. What he abolishes is the Gentile pattern in which power is used over others and then dressed up as generosity. Among his people the leader takes the place of the youngest and the servant.

The first test of a shepherd is how he comes to the flock. Authority over God's people that is seized, whether by force or by stealth, is illegitimate however religious its language, and the chapter measures every leader by the one who enters by the gate.

The hired hand's failure is not that he is paid but that the sheep are not his and his own safety comes first. The test of a leader of God's people is what he does when the wolf comes. The New Testament uses the same image of wolves among the flock (Acts 20:29) and calls elders to shepherd willingly and not for gain (1 Peter 5:2).

The Lord takes the place of a slave with a towel and basin. The scene makes service the defining form of authority among his followers, a point Jesus will draw out in verses 12-17 and that Peter later puts in the image of clothing oneself with humility (1 Peter 5:5).

Jesus does not give up his titles; he affirms them (verse 13) and then shows what they mean. Authority among his followers is measured by readiness to serve, the lesson Luke records at the same supper (Luke 22:25-27).

The risen Shepherd entrusts his own sheep to an under-shepherd. The church's leaders shepherd a flock that belongs to Christ and answer to him for it, which is how Paul charges the Ephesian elders (Acts 20:28) and how 1 Peter 5:1-4 charges elders under the chief Shepherd. Churches differ on how far this charge was unique to Peter.

The one who failed most publicly is given the care of the flock. Leadership in Christ's church rests on grace received, not on a record without failure; Peter's later exhortation to humble shepherding (1 Peter 5:2-5) comes from a man who knew this morning.

Paul presents Timothy's authority as coming from proven character and shared servanthood, not position. The broken father and son image insists that apostle and coworker stand together under the gospel.
Paul's labor is real and exhausting, yet the power in it is God's. The pattern for Christian leadership is hard work that depends entirely on God's working.
